title: Explaining Research Findings with Confidence
teaching_need: Undergraduates often struggle to turn research evidence into a clear, accurate explanation for non-specialists—mixing findings with interpretation, overstating certainty, and improving work without developing evaluative judgement.
intended_capability: Interpret and communicate a research finding accurately and appropriately for a non-specialist audience, and improve an explanation through comparison, self-diagnosis and reasoned revision.
summary: A 90-minute Learning Journey in which learners interpret a self-contained research study, write a first explanation, compare contrasting examples against quality criteria, diagnose and revise their own work, then account for what changed—supported by a Learning Journal that preserves learner-authored artefacts.
primary_pattern: Evaluative judgement through comparison, self-diagnosis and revision (draft → judge → revise)
supporting_patterns: Initial independent performance before worked examples or detailed evaluative guidance
Comparison of contrasting explanations against explicit quality criteria
Self-assessment and diagnosis of own work
Iterative improvement of a retained first attempt
Reflection on changes made and why they matter
Learning Journal preserving learner-authored work across the sequence
learning_sequence: Overview — orientation to the journey and expectations
Interpret the research evidence (Interactive) — build understanding of a self-contained illustrative study
Write your first explanation (Assessment Pack) — independent explanation for a non-specialist reader, retained as a baseline
Compare explanations and judge their quality (Interactive) — contrast examples and practise comparative judgement
Diagnose your explanation (Assessment Pack) — apply criteria to your own first attempt
Revise your explanation (Assessment Pack) — improve the retained baseline in light of diagnosis
Explain what changed and why (Expository) — account for revisions and their significance
Learning Journal — preserve and revisit learner-authored work across the journey
transferable_principle: When the goal is evaluative judgement rather than a single correct answer, have learners produce an independent attempt first, then use comparison against explicit criteria, self-diagnosis and revision—preserving the original work so improvement can be reasoned about. The subject matter and exact activities can change; the draft–judge–revise logic travels.
